entries.abstract: # Agents SDK v0.24.0-alpha.8 ## Highlights - **Approve Python tool calls before they run.** Review the arguments and approve or reject the call. You can remember a decision for the rest of the Session. [Managed approval example](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/managed_approvals/README.md#inspect-and-decide) - **Connect your own model client.** The native tool loop works with async Responses and Chat Completions clients, LiteLLM, AnyLLM, and custom adapters. [Application-owned model clients](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/models.md#use-an-application-owned-model-client) - **Add Realtime voice to a Session.** Use a server WebSocket, connect a browser over WebRTC, or attach to an existing SIP call. [Realtime connection options](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/native_voice.md#choose-a-connection) - **Resume more kinds of work.** Save supported pending tool requests and approvals. Request and token budgets keep the usage already spent when you restore a supported checkpoint. [Restore a checkpoint with a budget](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/budgeted-recovery.md) - **Install on more Linux systems.** The preview adds an ARM64 wheel. Both Linux wheels support glibc 2.28 or newer. [Preview wheel platform requirements](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/.github/RELEASING.md#L44) ## Added - Observe tool-search calls, tool-search results, and hosted MCP approval decisions through `ModelOutputItemCompleted`. Use `include_execution_details=True` to receive full items; receive summaries by default. [Live tool observations](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/packages/codex/src/_agents_codex/observation.py#L238-L267) - Use native Session Realtime APIs from `agents.realtime.native`, including `RealtimeAgentConfig(is_tool_enabled=...)`. Keep retained Classic/v0 Realtime imports under `agents.realtime`. [Native voice](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/native_voice.md#choose-a-connection) · [Classic imports](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/CLASSIC.md#compatible-voice-and-realtime-imports) - Handle managed function approvals with `FunctionToolApprovalRequest` and `FunctionToolApprovalDecision`. Set `run_input_policy_before_approval=True` to run the input policy before the approval predicate as well as before execution. Return `FinishTurn(output)` from `tool_batch_completion` to propose a final value with output validation and completion checks. [Managed approvals](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/managed_approvals/README.md#inspect-and-decide) · [Finish a tool batch](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/outputs.md#finish-after-a-tool-batch) - Create a remote conversation only when needed with `ConversationsHistory.ensure_conversation_id()`. Preserve a checked history prefix with `Session.replace_history_suffix(keep_prefix_count=...)`, and append staged checkpoint input with `SessionState.with_appended_pending_input()`. Read Unix milliseconds from `StoredTurn.started_at_ms` and `completed_at_ms`. [History APIs](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/reference.md#history-and-storage-apis) · [History edits](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#read-and-edit-original-history) - Use `SQLAlchemySQLiteSessionStore` for an application-owned synchronous SQLite engine, and `ResponsesSocketFactoryOptions` for resolved WebSocket connection parameters. Read received logprob data through `TextLogprobsFact`, `TokenLogprob`, `TokenLogprobAlternative`, and `MalformedLogprobsFact`, with unchanged serialized record kinds. Import `ModelRunOwner` from `agents.models` and `ApplicationToolOutput` from `agents.state`. [SQLite storage](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#sqlalchemy-sqlite-storage) · [Model ownership and socket options](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/reference.md#model-run-ownership-and-websocket-options) · [Logprob facts](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/streaming.md#inspect-provider-logprobs) - Group prompt-cache routing for fresh Sessions with an explicit `TraceOptions.group_id`. Keep the saved cache key when restoring a Session. Set a borrowed model adapter's `prompt_cache_key` to override only that adapter's outgoing key. Treat routing as affinity without a guaranteed cache hit. [Prompt-cache routing](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/observability.md#prompt-cache-routing-for-fresh-sessions) - Route work through native handoffs or call a specialist with `Agent.as_tool()`. Add input and output guardrails, or use `Agent.decide()` for a separate typed decision with explicit input. [Handoffs](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/sessions.md#hand-off-the-conversation-to-another-agent) · [Typed decisions](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/decisions-guide.md) - Use standalone Python function tools and select MCP tools by alias. Defer eligible tool schemas with `ToolSearch`. Function tools also support strict schemas, output schemas, and an option to ignore extra arguments. [Python tool declarations](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/tools.md#python-functions) · [Tool schema discovery](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/tools.md#discover-tool-schemas) - Use Redis, MongoDB, SQLAlchemy, or a Dapr Redis state component to store supported root conversations through `CustomStorage`. Compatible Responses providers also support provider-managed conversation history. [Application-owned storage](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#store-history-in-an-application-backend) - Use ordinary manual `FunctionTool` requests and preapproved `HttpMCP` tools with `CustomStorage`. Suspend a supported manual request and restore into independent memory. To continue through the original backend, use an unchanged checkpoint with one unresolved ordinary manual call. Keep managed function approvals, pending MCP requests, and staged input outside that same-backend restore path. [CustomStorage support and checkpoint limits](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#store-history-in-an-application-backend) - Open read-only execution environments, supply skills, or implement command and patch tools with application callbacks. Callbacks run with the application's permissions. [Read-only workspaces](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/execution.md#inspect-a-read-only-workspace) · [Native skills](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/execution.md#supply-native-skills) - Set per-request model options for sampling, retries, deadlines, and prompt caching. Request produced items and history from one-shot runs, or opt in to provider reasoning summaries and tool-argument deltas. [Model request controls](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/models.md#model-request-controls) · [Streaming and retained history](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/streaming.md#inspect-observations-and-retained-history) ## Changed - Native streaming HTTP can negotiate HTTP/2. Buffered Responses continue to use HTTP/1.1. - Set `NativeProvider(tool_output_token_limit=...)` to adjust the approximate tool-result budget for model context. Leave it unset to use the model's default. The setting is separate from the final answer limit. [Tool output limit reference](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/packages/codex/src/_agents_codex/agent.py#L488-L497) ## Fixed - Reject invalid web-starter request bodies and prompts before admitting work. Reject deeply nested JSON, non-object bodies, and text without valid UTF-8 encoding. [Web-starter request validation](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/web_starter/app.py#L433-L474) - Wait for confirmed remote command exit during cancellation. Report a failure when the executor acknowledges a stop without confirming exit. - Preserve the backing store's configured history limit when a Classic compaction wrapper has no explicit settings. Explicit wrapper and per-run limits still take precedence. - Strict Python tools return a retryable error to the model when the original arguments fail validation, before approval or callback execution. A corrected call still goes through approval when required. [Function argument validation reference](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/packages/codex/src/_agents_codex/_function_tools.py#L1390-L1404) - Preserve completed tool results during supported checkpoint restores. Report uncertain calls for reconciliation before reopening local profiles with interrupted child work. [Recover after an interruption](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#recover-after-interruption) - Preserve accepted model settings and history across supported handoffs and retries. Improve provider error reporting so applications can see where a request failed. [Inspect provider response attempts](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/streaming.md#inspect-response-attempts) - Harden protection for native workspace metadata and credential files. Reduce startup work for simple runs and reuse eligible HTTP connections. ## Upgrading from 0.24.0-alpha.7 - Use the alpha.8 wheel for the features in these notes. Some linked guides still refer to development builds. If an example needs files from the repository, use the revision linked in these notes. Alpha.7 does not accept newer keywords such as `strict` on `function_tool` or `model_backend` on `NativeProvider`. - For Linux local execution, install `bubblewrap` with a compatible `bwrap` in `/usr/bin` or `/bin` and allow sandbox namespace creation. For a Linux Docker executor, supply `bwrap` in the container image or executor bundle. [Linux executor setup](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/execution.md#local-execution) - **Back up your saved state before upgrading.** Alpha.7 supports budgets for live runs. Alpha.8 adds checkpointing for supported pending runs with request or token budgets. The checkpoint saves the requests or tokens already used so they still count after restore. Alpha.7 rejects this new format because it cannot enforce the saved budget. We verified that both versions can reopen idle checkpoints, checkpoints waiting for a manual Python tool reply, and closed `LocalStorage` profiles on Linux x86-64. These checks used matching app settings and features available in both versions. If alpha.7 cannot reopen your saved state after rollback, restore your pre-upgrade backup. [Resume a budgeted checkpoint](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/examples/codex/budgeted-recovery.md) · [Checkpoint restore setup](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#supply-restore-configuration) · [Reopen a local profile](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/state.md#reopen-a-conversation-from-local-storage) - Replace bare `"*"` entries in network domain rules with exact hosts or scoped patterns such as `"*.example.org"`. To allow outbound public hosts, use `NetworkPolicy.allow_all()`. On Linux, this also requires `allow_all_unix_sockets=True` and an executor isolated from host services and other jobs. Explicit network policies remain unsupported on Windows. [Network policy and platform limits](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/execution.md#network-and-local-socket-access) - If you relied on a saved Codex login to enable ChatGPT Apps tools, add the existing `ChatGPTAppsMCP` declaration to the Agent's tools. Supply the provisioned Apps token, its account ID, and the tool names you want to expose. A saved Codex login now supplies model authentication only. [ChatGPT Apps setup](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/mcp.md#connect-personal-chatgpt-apps) - If your code reads `session.items()`, count each execution once. Provider `function_call` and `function_call_output` rows can accompany a typed record for the same execution. Match native `thread_id`, `turn_id`, and `call_id` rather than counting rows or relying on a history cursor's `id`. Recheck saved-history readers and analytics before upgrading. [Execution history](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/docs/sdk/streaming.md#inspect-completed-execution) - If you use Classic `WorkspaceJsonlSink`, choose a log budget before upgrading. Its default is now 8 MiB. Exceeding the existing-file or pending-buffer budget drops pending events and permanently stops that sink; rebinding does not restart it. Create a new sink for a new outbox or a larger finite `max_bytes`, or use `JsonlOutboxSink` or `HttpProxySink` outside the workspace for long-lived logs. Use `max_bytes=None` only for trusted workloads that need unlimited reads. The sink does not rotate or truncate logs. [Workspace sink limits](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/src/agents/classic/sandbox/session/sinks.py#L143-L186) - If you use the `classic-blaxel` extra and pin Blaxel, update the pin to `0.2.51` or newer. Test saved sandbox restoration with your current network and port settings. Blaxel, Cloudflare, Daytona, E2B, Modal, and Vercel can now reject saved settings that conflict with the current policy. Create a fresh sandbox with the required settings instead of relaxing the policy to reuse old state. [Blaxel dependency](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/pyproject.toml#L113-L117) · [Example restore-policy check](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e/src/agents/classic/extensions/sandbox/blaxel/sandbox.py#L1095-L1102) ## Release verification Source: [`d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/commit/d6a81c997eabdc56108633eb3132fb3907f87d7e). Built and tested by [Tests #43800450653](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/actions/runs/43800450653). Verified fresh installs on all four platforms with CPython 3.10 and 3.14. [Installation checks](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/actions/runs/43805410415)

entries.abstract: This release restores a working install, fixes a published security vulnerability, and makes Ragas work again with current OpenAI and Anthropic models. ```bash pip install -U ragas ``` ## Highlights - **`import ragas` works again.** A fresh install pulled in `langchain-community` 0.4, which removed the VertexAI modules Ragas imported at start-up, so the import failed with `ModuleNotFoundError`. Those imports are now optional. (#2956) - **Security fix for multimodal metrics (CVE-2026-6587).** See the security section below. (#3105) - **Anthropic works on current Claude models.** Ragas no longer sends the sampling defaults that current models reject, and it no longer forces a tool call that the newest models refuse. (#3106, #3108) - **OpenAI models with dotted versions work.** `gpt-5.2` and similar are now recognised, so `max_tokens` is sent as `max_completion_tokens`. (#2700) - **OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock work.** Bedrock model IDs such as `us.openai.gpt-6-sol` are now recognised as reasoning models, so they no longer fail with a 400. (#3049) - **Synchronous clients work in async metrics.** `agenerate()` with a sync client runs in a thread instead of raising `TypeError`. (#2657) - **Deprecation warnings point to imports that exist.** 22 of the warnings in `ragas.metrics` suggested a `ragas.metrics.collections` import that raised `ImportError`. (#2974) ## Security `MultiModalFaithfulness` and `MultiModalRelevance` load images named in `retrieved_contexts`. A context string could make the machine running the evaluation fetch an internal URL (for example a cloud metadata endpoint) or read a local image file, and send the result to the LLM provider. This is CVE-2026-6587 / GHSA-95ww-475f-pr4f. Both the collections API and the legacy API are fixed: - Image URLs are fetched only from public internet addresses. The check runs on the address actually connected to, on every redirect, so redirects and DNS rebinding do not get around it. - Local image paths are not read unless you enable local file access and name the one directory images may be loaded from. If you use these metrics with untrusted datasets, upgrade. Thanks to @GeoffreyManda, whose fix and tests in #3089 this builds on, and to the reporters in #2754. ## Changes you may notice **Multimodal metrics** - Local image paths in `retrieved_contexts` are no longer loaded by default in the collections API. An image that is not loaded is passed to the model as text and a warning is logged, so check your logs if scores change. - Image URLs on `localhost` or private addresses are refused in both APIs. - To opt back in, set these before running the metric: ```python import ragas.prompt.multi_modal_prompt as image_policy # Read local images, but only from inside this directory image_policy.ALLOW_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS = True image_policy.ALLOWED_IMAGE_BASE_DIR = "/data/eval_images" # Allow image URLs on internal or private addresses image_policy.ALLOW_INTERNAL_TARGETS = True ``` - The metric pages document the rules and settings in full: [MultiModalFaithfulness](https://docs.ragas.io/en/latest/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/multi_modal_faithfulness/#image-loading-and-security) and [MultiModalRelevance](https://docs.ragas.io/en/latest/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/multi_modal_relevance/#image-loading-and-security). **Anthropic (`llm_factory(..., provider="anthropic")`)** - `temperature` and `top_p` are no longer sent unless you set them. Older Claude models that accepted Ragas' defaults (`temperature=0.01`, `top_p=0.1`) now run at the API's default temperature, so scores can vary more between runs. - The default structured-output mode is now JSON mode instead of a forced tool call. Pass `mode=instructor.Mode.TOOLS` to keep the old behaviour on models that accept it. - An explicit `mode=` now reaches Anthropic, Google and Perplexity. It was silently ignored before. **Dependencies** - `requests` and `tenacity` are now declared as core dependencies. Ragas already imported both. ## Known issues - Version 2.x of the `anthropic` package no longer accepts `temperature` or `top_p`. Setting either on an Anthropic model raises an error from the SDK. - Claude models reached through LiteLLM still receive Ragas' default sampling parameters. - Behind an HTTP proxy, the image URL check cannot see the final address for hostnames that only the proxy can resolve. ## What's Changed * docs: fix Install docs dependencies by @injaeryou in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2564 * fix: detect and handle OpenAI-compatible API style for generic providers (deepseek, groq, xai, etc) by @anistark in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2561 * docs: fix readme's quickstart and quickstart link by @injaeryou in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2563 * feat: add mode parameter to llm_factory for custom instructor modes by @anistark in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2565 * perf: optimize average precision algorithm by @minimAluminiumalism in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2567 * fix: fix testset generation bugs by @kraftn in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2568 * chore: remove office hours cal by @anistark in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2583 * fix: allow fork contributors in check-docs CI workflow by @veeceey in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2606 * fix(llms): make VertexAI imports optional for langchain-community >= 0.4 by @sanyaden in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2956 * ci: repair CI after dependency drift by @harshil-sanghvi in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/3092 * fix(security): guard multimodal image loading against SSRF and local file reads (CVE-2026-6587) by @jjmachan and @GeoffreyManda in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/3105 * fix(llms): stop sending default sampling params to Anthropic and forward an explicit mode by @jjmachan in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/3106 * ci: verify the release before uploading to PyPI by @jjmachan in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/3107 * fix(llms): default Anthropic to JSON mode by @jjmachan in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/3108 * Handle decimal GPT versions in OpenAI token mapping by @mindbomber in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2700 * fix: allow agenerate to work with sync clients via thread pool by @devsvarun in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2657 * docs: mark the multimodal image loading change as new in 0.4.4 by @jjmachan in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/3109 * docs: build the docs with the public mkdocs-material package by @jjmachan in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/3110 * fix(llms): map Bedrock reasoning model IDs by @mikamikasuki in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/3049 * fix: point deprecation warnings to correct collections metric names by @BenBrahimMazen in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2974 ## New Contributors * @injaeryou made their first contribution in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2564 * @minimAluminiumalism made their first contribution in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2567 * @kraftn made their first contribution in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2568 * @veeceey made their first contribution in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2606 * @sanyaden made their first contribution in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2956 * @mindbomber made their first contribution in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2700 * @devsvarun made their first contribution in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2657 * @mikamikasuki made their first contribution in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/3049 * @BenBrahimMazen made their first contribution in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2974 **Full Changelog**: entries.abstract: This is a release candidate for 0.4.4. It restores a working install, fixes a published security vulnerability, and makes Ragas work again with current OpenAI and Anthropic models. Please try it and report anything that breaks before the final release. ```bash pip install --pre ragas==0.4.4rc1 ``` ## Highlights - **`import ragas` works again.** A fresh install pulled in `langchain-community` 0.4, which removed the VertexAI modules Ragas imported at start-up, so the import failed with `ModuleNotFoundError`. Those imports are now optional. (#2956) - **Security fix for multimodal metrics (CVE-2026-6587).** See the security section below. (#3105) - **Anthropic works on current Claude models.** Ragas no longer sends the sampling defaults that current models reject, and it no longer forces a tool call that the newest models refuse. (#3106, #3108) - **OpenAI models with dotted versions work.** `gpt-5.2` and similar are now recognised, so `max_tokens` is sent as `max_completion_tokens`. (#2700) - **Synchronous clients work in async metrics.** `agenerate()` with a sync client runs in a thread instead of raising `TypeError`. (#2657) ## Security `MultiModalFaithfulness` and `MultiModalRelevance` load images named in `retrieved_contexts`. A context string could make the machine running the evaluation fetch an internal URL (for example a cloud metadata endpoint) or read a local image file, and send the result to the LLM provider. This is CVE-2026-6587 / GHSA-95ww-475f-pr4f. Both the collections API and the legacy API are fixed: - Image URLs are fetched only from public internet addresses. The check runs on the address actually connected to, on every redirect, so redirects and DNS rebinding do not get around it. - Local image paths are not read unless you enable local file access and name the one directory images may be loaded from. If you use these metrics with untrusted datasets, upgrade. Thanks to @GeoffreyManda, whose fix and tests in #3089 this builds on, and to the reporters in #2754. ## Changes you may notice **Multimodal metrics** - Local image paths in `retrieved_contexts` are no longer loaded by default in the collections API. An image that is not loaded is passed to the model as text and a warning is logged, so check your logs if scores change. - Image URLs on `localhost` or private addresses are refused in both APIs. - To opt back in, set these before running the metric: ```python import ragas.prompt.multi_modal_prompt as image_policy # Read local images, but only from inside this directory image_policy.ALLOW_LOCAL_FILE_ACCESS = True image_policy.ALLOWED_IMAGE_BASE_DIR = "/data/eval_images" # Allow image URLs on internal or private addresses image_policy.ALLOW_INTERNAL_TARGETS = True ``` - The metric pages document the rules and settings in full: [MultiModalFaithfulness](https://docs.ragas.io/en/latest/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/multi_modal_faithfulness/#image-loading-and-security) and [MultiModalRelevance](https://docs.ragas.io/en/latest/concepts/metrics/available_metrics/multi_modal_relevance/#image-loading-and-security). **Anthropic (`llm_factory(..., provider="anthropic")`)** - `temperature` and `top_p` are no longer sent unless you set them. Older Claude models that accepted Ragas' defaults (`temperature=0.01`, `top_p=0.1`) now run at the API's default temperature, so scores can vary more between runs. - The default structured-output mode is now JSON mode instead of a forced tool call. Pass `mode=instructor.Mode.TOOLS` to keep the old behaviour on models that accept it. - An explicit `mode=` now reaches Anthropic, Google and Perplexity. It was silently ignored before. **Dependencies** - `requests` and `tenacity` are now declared as core dependencies. Ragas already imported both. ## Known issues - Version 2.x of the `anthropic` package no longer accepts `temperature` or `top_p`. Setting either on an Anthropic model raises an error from the SDK. - Claude models reached through LiteLLM still receive Ragas' default sampling parameters. - Behind an HTTP proxy, the image URL check cannot see the final address for hostnames that only the proxy can resolve. ## What's Changed * docs: fix Install docs dependencies by @injaeryou in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2564 * fix: detect and handle OpenAI-compatible API style for generic providers (deepseek, groq, xai, etc) by @anistark in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2561 * docs: fix readme's quickstart and quickstart link by @injaeryou in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2563 * feat: add mode parameter to llm_factory for custom instructor modes by @anistark in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2565 * perf: optimize average precision algorithm by @minimAluminiumalism in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2567 * fix: fix testset generation bugs by @kraftn in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2568 * chore: remove office hours cal by @anistark in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2583 * fix: allow fork contributors in check-docs CI workflow by @veeceey in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2606 * fix(llms): make VertexAI imports optional for langchain-community >= 0.4 by @sanyaden in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/2956 * ci: repair CI after dependency drift by @harshil-sanghvi in https://github.com/vibrantlabsai/ragas/pull/3092 * fix(security): guard multimodal image entries.abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.
entries.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots

entries.abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.
entries.comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Code and leaderboard available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench
entries.title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers

entries.abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
entries.comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Code, videos and results: https://zhanghutony.github.io/ibmarl/. A preliminary version appeared at the PhysCollaBot Workshop at IROS 2026
entries.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

entries.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly relies on a harness, the scaffold around the model that decides what it sees of its own interaction and what guidance it receives. Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL, which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State, a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model's behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task's data and evolved with the model.
entries.title: ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL

entries.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.
entries.title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection

entries.abstract: Lagrangian particle tracking follows virtual particles in the velocity fields of an ocean model to study transport pathways, connectivity and dispersion. Setting up such a study takes many technical steps, and this work is increasingly done with coding agents, programs in which a language model writes code, runs it and checks the result. We present KELP v1.0, the Kinematic Engine for Lagrangian Particles, a tracker for unstructured ocean-model meshes and HEALPix grids that is built to be operated by such agents. KELP computes two- and three-dimensional trajectories with established methods on triangular, quadrilateral and mixed meshes, with global FESOM2 and coastal FESOM-C meshes as examples, and on HEALPix, the equal-area grid on which kilometre-scale digital twins distribute their output. Documentation and short task instructions, called skills, tell an agent how to prepare releases and configurations, run calculations and process the trajectories. An agent prepared and ran all experiments of this paper with these skills, and most of the preparation was completed within hours. In a controlled evaluation, the skills raised the completeness of study files prepared by five language models from 75-93% to 88-100%. KELP reproduced the particle distributions of two other trackers on the same fields. Trajectories on HEALPix fields converged to those on the model mesh as the pixels were refined. After one year, the median distance between the two was 1.6 km at a pixel spacing of 25.5 km. HEALPix output can therefore be used for Lagrangian studies of ensemble statistics when the original mesh is not available. In a 63-year calculation with 7.92 million particles released in the Beaufort Gyre, transport from the gyre to Fram Strait took years to decades, and the run took 3 h 36 min on one 128-core node. A test tracked $10^{10}$ particles on a HEALPix mesh of 35.5 million wet surface nodes.
entries.title: KELP v1.0: an agent-ready Lagrangian particle tracker for unstructured meshes and HEALPix grids

entries.abstract: Physical design automation of very large-scale integrated circuits (VLSI) has made significant strides, progressing from single-stage placement and routing toward increasingly integrated full-flow implementation. Yet, existing approaches struggle with the vast design space optimization (DSO) arising from diverse technology nodes, circuit designs, and varied constraints. The substantial runtime of physical-design tools further exacerbates this challenge, leaving industrial workflows heavily dependent on experienced engineers to navigate the design space and achieve power, performance, and area (PPA) targets, incurring significant engineering effort. We argue that large language models (LLMs) with strong reasoning capabilities, enriched with distilled human design expertise, offer a promising path toward efficient and automated DSO. Unlike traditional algorithms, LLMs can interpret complex design contexts and naturally incorporate human expertise expressed in natural language for reasoning, acting, observing, and adapting throughout the design process, a capability that conventional optimization methods cannot exploit. To this end, we present OpenLayout, an agentic platform that leverages multi-agent collaboration with embedded design knowledge to enable self-iterative DSO. We further introduce OpenLayout-Bench, a benchmark targeting advanced technology nodes with commercial EDA tools to systematically evaluate physical design automation capabilities of LLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that OpenLayout achieves state-of-the-art performance, with approximately 20% accuracy improvement over baseline methods. Our work is open-sourced at https://github.com/fenggev56/OpenLayout
entries.title: OpenLayout: An Open and Agentic-Driven Platform for Holistic VLSI Physical Design and Benchmarking

entries.abstract: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. OCR-based indexing is fast but loses visual information; visual encoding takes over two seconds. Yet screens change incrementally: most pixels repeat within and across screenshots. This raises a question: do visual encoders need to recompute their representations from scratch for every new screenshot? We present StreamEmbed, a system for incremental visual embedding that exploits this redundancy. Guided solely by pixel differences, it combines spatial token pruning, which skips blocks that repeat a neighbor, with temporal KV reuse, which reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged across screenshots. A small learned adapter compensates for pruning and reuse to preserve fidelity to full-screenshot embeddings. On ScreenMemEval, our benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen histories from two humans and a computer-use agent, StreamEmbed sets a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on an M2 Pro GPU: it encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding without sacrificing accuracy and improves accuracy over OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. A memory-efficient vector index stores a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM. Together, these results make real-time indexing of screen history in its native visual form practical, laying a foundation for fully local visual assistants.
entries.title: StreamEmbed: Real-Time Indexing from Pixels for Screenshot Retrieval

entries.abstract: This work addresses the fundamental question concerning the nature of quantum states, specifically to what extent they represent an agent's knowledge about the system, that is, is \textit{epistemic} in nature. We show that, despite the existence of the Kochen-Specker model, which is a maximally $ψ-$epistemic model for single-qubit systems when projective measurements are employed, \textit{no} maximally $ψ-$epistemic model can reproduce statistics arising out of non-projective measurements on a pair of single-qubit states. This has been done in an experimentally robust way using only two pure single-qubit states and their equal mixture, by constructing a two-input, three-output game called \textit{Risk Aware Distinguishability} (RAD) and generalizing the notion of epistemic and quantum overlaps using RAD. Furthermore, we maximize the difference of generalized overlaps instead of minimizing their ratio, and in the process point out why that is a stricter criterion for refuting $ψ-$epistemic models.
entries.title: No-go theorem for maximally $ψ-$epistemic models using two pure states of a qubit

entries.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.
entries.title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination

entries.abstract: Common data elements (CDEs) support clinical data comparability but are usually defined manually. We investigated whether large language model agents could derive a CDE schema from sarcoma case report abstracts and apply it at scale. An agent proposed 72,909 candidate CDEs from 24,588 PubMed abstracts; agentic consolidation yielded 1,570 CDEs. We retained 53 supported by at least 50 abstracts and attempted evidence-linked extraction across the corpus. Processing succeeded for all retained CDEs in 79.2% of abstracts, including responses indicating non-mention. Two human reviewers approved 83.0% of retained CDEs for relevance, 67.9% for clarity, and 56.6% for correctness. In 100 sampled abstracts, exact agreement with the value extracted by the LLM was 94.9% among 1,116 pairs with a non-empty answer (abstract-level bootstrap 95% CI, 93.0-96.4%). Errors concentrated in anatomical and temporal fields. These findings support agent-assisted schema drafting followed by expert curation before large-scale extraction.
entries.title: Agentic induction of common data elements and information extraction from sarcoma case report abstracts

entries.abstract: Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.
entries.title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits

entries.abstract: Agentic time series forecasting extends conventional approaches beyond one-shot numerical prediction toward autonomous, context-aware interaction. However, existing benchmarks offer limited integrated support for diverse contextual information, forecasting-specific adaptive interactions, and systematic evaluation of forecasting agents. In this paper, we introduce CastWorld, an agentic benchmark for context-aware time series forecasting. First, its context-rich dataset suite spans 8 domains and 25 real-world datasets, covering external variables, events, and historical cases under a unified context specification. Second, a lightweight, modular forecasting-native harness provides 49 core tools and a state-adaptive loop that tracks forecast versions and enables iterative evidence gathering and forecast revision. Intermediate forecasts can expose information gaps, while newly acquired evidence guides subsequent revisions and final version selection. Third, model-level evaluation assesses forecast quality, process execution, behavioral trustworthiness, and resource efficiency through decision trajectories and forecast-version histories. Also, systems-level evaluation compares predictive accuracy across forecasting systems. Experiments reveal distinct decision behaviors among agents with comparable accuracy. Additional interactions do not necessarily improve forecasts, and agents may fail to select their best previously generated predictions. Allowing evidence acquisition during forecast refinement improves task-aware forecast scores across all three evaluated models. CastWorld provides a reusable foundation for evaluating agentic time series forecasting under controlled conditions.
entries.title: CastWorld: Benchmarking Context-Aware Agentic Time Series Forecasting Beyond Predictive Accuracy

entries.abstract: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.
entries.comment: 21 pages, 5 figures. Code and saved results: https://github.com/tokencraftdata/agentic-compliance
entries.title: TradeGauntlet: Evaluating Compliance Controls for Autonomous Trading Agents

entries.abstract: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}γ\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.
entries.title: Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors

entries.abstract: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.
entries.comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems, Volume 10 (2027)
entries.title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration

entries.abstract: LLM agents increasingly act over long horizons, where outcome-only rewards say little about which intermediate actions were good. Dense supervision methods address this by scoring intermediate steps, but they are usually evaluated through the downstream performance of a full training pipeline. This is expensive, confounds signal quality with other training choices, and means that methods are rarely compared on common ground. We introduce QVal, a training-free testbed that measures the $Q$-alignment of a dense signal: whether it orders the candidate actions in each state the same way as their returns under a reference policy do. We benchmark 21 methods from seven families with six open-weight backbones in four environments. Simple prompting baselines are the most $Q$-aligned on average, and performance clusters strongly by family. Code-generated signals do well only in small state and action spaces; embedding-based signals are weak; self-distillation signals are anti-aligned; and no method is $Q$-aligned in open-ended environments. When five of these signals guide an actor at test time by choosing among four proposed actions, $Q$-alignment strongly correlates with the gain in task success. QVal is designed to be easily extensible to new environments and methods, enabling researchers to compare new signals cheaply before committing to a training run.
entries.comment: 10 pages, 6 figures in main text; 67 pages, 13 figures with appendix
entries.title: QVal: Evaluating Dense Supervision Signals for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

entries.abstract: AI agents are trained on population-scale data to encode broad capabilities spanning those of many practitioners. Yet the artifacts they produce rarely meet the personal bar professionals need to stake their reputation on. On realistic, open-ended tasks where success criteria are heterogeneous and insufficiently documented, individual expertise lives precisely in the elevation and departure from the average. In practice, iterative human-agent interaction surfaces criteria that users cannot fully specify up front, yet apply repeatedly across tasks. We argue this cross-session interaction data is a rich, underused signal for closing the gap to individual expertise. In this work, we propose test-time adaptation through human-agent interaction (TAHI), which integrates these signals into agent context and weights, and crystallizes each user's training and evaluation criteria via an evolving rubric module. We adapt agents to 30 individuals in two high-utility domains, writing and visual creation, on a total of 600 tasks. Our agents improve solo task success by 4.5-20.9% within only tens of tasks. Meanwhile, our evolving rubric module serves as a scalable annotation tool, creating evaluation rubrics that catch 16.0-22.3% more failures than those from LMs or humans alone. While agents are adapted towards individuals, we show these personalized agents also produce improvements in success of up to 8.8% that generalize across users.
entries.title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation through Human-Agent Interaction

entries.abstract: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development
entries.title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation

entries.abstract: The questions of voting rights, group membership, and the boundaries of acceptable discourse all involve a recursive, self-stability issue, wherein the voters, group members, and acceptable commentators are often the ultimate arbiters of their own rules for inclusion and exclusion. In order to understand how ideological or issue diversity may impact the stability of such inclusion and exclusion, we introduce franchise elections, where voting members of a group vote to change the electorate. In particular, when agents are positioned inside an ideological or issue space, a social choice function that aggregates agent viewpoints induces a preference for agents over group composition, where agents prefer groups that improve the social choice function outcome for them. We demonstrate that when ideological space is two-dimensional, these franchise elections can generate complex behavior and that this complexity exists for any social choice function. Using the Yolk social choice function from voting theory, we illustrate that franchise elections can predict that agents attempting to introduce a new ideological axis perpendicular to an existing left-right spectrum risk disenfranchisement unless they ally with either side of the spectrum, and that franchise elections can cycle with any period.
entries.title: Disenfranchisement in Spatial Voting Games

entries.abstract: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.
entries.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation

entries.abstract: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP mean absolute error of 7.3 mmHg, compared with 9.2 mmHg for random selection at the same coverage. The gated agent achieves 60.0% agreement with recorded actions at 81.0% decision coverage, compared with 55.0% agreement and 99.5% coverage for an ungated ensemble agent. Component ablations show lower factual risk with joint gating than with either gate alone.These results characterize a reliability--coverage trade-off in selective clinical simulation; they do not identify individualized treatment effects or establish improved patient outcomes.
entries.title: When to Trust Simulated Patient Responses:Support-Gated World Models for Vasopressor Decision Support

entries.abstract: Modern coding agents rely on establishing executable software environments before they can perform software engineering tasks such as testing, debugging, and patch validation. Existing setup agents typically control progress at either single-command or whole-script granularity, making recovery either too local to remove polluted state or too coarse to preserve useful progress. We present HerAgent (Harness EnviRonment Setup Agent), a block-level harness for coding-agent environment setup. HerAgent's main contribution is semantic setup blocks: a single progress-control abstraction used for execution, validation, checkpointing, repair, and rollback. Evaluated against six prior agents on four environment-setup datasets, HerAgent improves setup success in every comparison, achieving the largest gains on Installamatic-Bench (52.0% to 85.0%) and SetupBench (46.3% to 70.4%). It also reduces setup costs by up to 94.5%, showing that block-level progress control improves reliability and efficiency.
entries.title: HerAgent: A Block-Level Checkpointing Harness for Coding-Agent Environment Setup

entries.abstract: Large language models increasingly use external tools such as web search and document retrieval to solve information-intensive tasks. However, multi-hop tool use in complex tasks introduces substantial latency, since the model must repeatedly wait for tool observations before continuing. We study how to accelerate such trajectories without changing the final trajectory the model would have taken without acceleration, assuming access to faster but less reliable speculator tools. We develop a theoretical framework for lossless speculation in multi-hop tool-use settings, characterizing the optimal achievable latency gain. We propose SpecHop, a continuous speculation framework that maintains multiple speculative threads, verifies predicted observations asynchronously as target tool outputs arrive, commits correct branches, and rolls back incorrect ones. This preserves accuracy while reducing wall-clock latency. We show that SpecHop can approach oracle latency gains with enough active threads. Empirically, on retrieval-augmented multi-hop tasks, SpecHop closely matches theoretical predictions and reduces latency by up to 40\% in some settings. Code: https://github.com/mehrdadsaberi/spechop
entries.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
entries.title: SpecHop: Continuous Speculation for Accelerating Multi-Hop Retrieval Agents

entries.abstract: Tool-calling agents are mostly optimized for accuracy; in deployment, however, their growing cost is latency: every tool call is decoded autoregressively. Speculative decoding accelerates this without changing the output, and retrieved past calls make strong drafts under real use, where each user's behavior tends to repeat. Yet existing systems keep no cross-session memory, or build the draft store once and never update it. We propose SpecMem, a tool-call memory kept alive and managed throughout deployment: verified calls are written back online into bounded per-user stores with LRU eviction, and a side-effect gate defers irreversible calls until verification confirms. On multi-session, multi-user query streams served by three open-weight models, a frozen store steadily loses acceptance while SpecMem holds it: a 27% gap in mean accepted tokens (+11% to +34% across benchmarks, tracking how much novel work arrives after the store is built) and up to 1.74x wall-clock speedup. Ablations attribute the gain almost entirely to keeping the store live; local per-user scoping adds no acceptance but closes a measured cross-user leakage channel, and gating on declared side effects, rather than on retrieval confidence, is what eliminates irreversible mistakes.
entries.title: SPECMEM: Accelerating Agentic Tool Calling via Live Memory Management

entries.abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.
entries.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent

entries.abstract: AI-enabled smart homes are becoming more common across the grid edge. However, there has not been much work on failure response. This area is critical because smart homes operate on the grid edge where failures can cascade down. If a power outage happens within a smart home, a user has to manually troubleshoot their smart home to include tasks such as power load balance and device recovery. We conduct the first resilience analysis of smart home agents across a full power outage, providing a suite of outage simulations in a live environment that measures resilience before, during, and post power outage. We show that smart home agents can act as grid operators in power outages and identify several new failure categories highlighting the current limitations across all of our models. These findings establish the groundwork for smart home agents as grid operators to increase overall resilience on the grid edge.
entries.comment: Pre-print. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
entries.title: Smart Home Agents Make Capable but Unpredictable Grid Operators

entries.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still requires extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable. Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/
entries.title: Self-Building Labs

entries.abstract: Generative AI enables voice-based conversational agents to play more active roles in older adults' care, including personalizing support and operating alongside clinicians and care partners. This shift creates two challenges: how to personalize support while faithfully delivering evidence-based interventions, and how to manage personal-data use and sharing across AI and care stakeholders. We designed and evaluated ARC, a voice-based conversational agent that operationalizes multidomain lifestyle intervention through sessions with predefined goals, participant context, and evidence-based components. In a 3-day remote study, 80 older adults completed 473 sessions across six session types (9,183 turns; averaging 19.4 turns and 6 minutes per session). Participants reported favorable usability, acceptability, and use intentions. System-level analyses showed strong domain-level but modest participant-specific contextual reuse, no significant personalization-fidelity association, and fidelity limitations centered on incomplete delivery of intervention components rather than off-protocol drift. Within care relationships, expectations for personal-data use and sharing varied by data type and recipient. Our findings support feasibility of conversational delivery of multidomain lifestyle intervention, offer methods and system-design insights for longitudinal evaluation, and motivate an evaluation agenda for generative AI health interventions: user-experience and outcome measures should be complemented by evidence of whether intended intervention processes were delivered as designed.
entries.title: Voice-Based Conversational Agents as AI Care Assistants: Evaluating Personalization, Intervention Delivery Fidelity, and Privacy Expectations in Older Adults' Care

entries.abstract: A generally intelligent system acquires new skills efficiently without requiring humans to redesign its software scaffold for every new task. Yet language models rarely act alone. A harness is a symbolic program that orchestrates calls to the model, handling perception, memory, tool use, recovery, and inference allocation on the model's behalf. ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive benchmark in which agents must explore unfamiliar environments, figure out their goals on the fly, and keep learning as they go. On it, human-steered systems already report ceiling scores across the public games, so we know effective designs exist. We ask whether frontier models can build and improve such a harness on their own. Through a fixed coding bootstrap, each model constructs a complete task harness, acts through that harness on five development games, and revises the entire codebase twice. Every version is evaluated on twenty games that never influence adaptation. We measure task performance with Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) and record dollar-denominated inference cost. Across 27 lineages, harness performance ranges from zero to near-ceiling scores. Two revisions raise mean held-out RHAE by only 2.80 points (95% interval [-1.44,7.35]). Development gains overstate held-out improvement, and reductions in inference cost can come at the expense of task performance. No revision retains its parent, yet a post hoc rule that selects among existing snapshots by development score raises the held-out gain to 4.53 points ([0.81,8.68]), separating the generation of revisions from the decision to deploy them. Human-steered systems demonstrate further headroom. These findings reveal a gap between autonomous harness construction and reliable adaptation under this two-revision protocol: even strong task performance does not ensure that subsequent revisions generalize or preserve existing capabilities.
entries.comment: 32 pages, 5 figures. Includes appendices and a supplementary code/data archive. v2: revised version with additional analyses
entries.title: Can LLMs Improve Their Own Harness? A Controlled Study on ARC-AGI-3

entries.abstract: Pseudo-inverse methods are widely used to solve control allocation problems for overactuated aircraft with redundant control effectors. These methods reliably satisfy the primary command tracking objective, while the remaining null-space degrees of freedom are in principle available for secondary objectives such as drag reduction or actuator wear balancing. However, exploiting this freedom in practice requires hand-tuned weighting matrices or a priori preferred deflections that are difficult to specify across a wide flight envelope with nonlinear, state-dependent dynamics. This paper presents a hybrid architecture in which a reinforcement learning agent operates exclusively within the null space of the control effectiveness matrix, learning secondary objective strategies directly from interaction with the flight dynamics. The null-space projector guarantees by construction that primary command tracking remains invariant regardless of the agent output, providing a principled separation between certified primary control and adaptive secondary optimization. The approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear six-degree-of-freedom distributed electric propulsion aircraft model with aero-propulsive effects across diverse mission scenarios, achieving measurable drag reduction compared to the baseline allocation while preserving tracking integrity and respecting actuator constraints. The proposed architecture forms a foundation for future extensions toward multi-objective, mission-conditioned policies.
entries.title: Reinforcement Learning for Null-Space Exploitation in Pseudo-Inverse Control Allocation

entries.abstract: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.
entries.title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes

entries.abstract: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics.
